newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel shrugs off Clinton criticism of settlements.
newsitem.headline: Israel shrugs off Clinton criticism of settlements.

text.p: A top Israeli official shrugged off criticism from U.S. President Bill Clinton on Jewish settlements, saying on Tuesday that Washington not Israel had to change its policy.
"The position of the administration on the settlements has been consistent," said David Bar-Illan, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's communications chief.

"They are opposed to any activity on the settlements and we have to try to change their minds but obviously we haven't been able to," he told Reuters, insisting that ties with Washington, Israel's closest ally, were still excellent.

Clinton on Monday embraced the tough language of his predecessor George Bush on the issue. Asked at the White House if he would call settlements an obstacle to peace, Clinton told reporters: "Absolutely".

Israeli-Palestinian tensions flared in the last week over Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to West Bank settlements. The cabinet action followed the killing of a settler mother and her son by Arab gunmen.

Bar-Illan voiced astonishment at reaction to the Israeli decision which he said was meant to eliminate discrimination against West Bank settlers by giving them benefits enjoyed by Israelis in other areas captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
He said a misunderstanding over the issue had to be cleared up.

A White House spokesman said Washington found the latest policy on settlements "a complicating factor" in peace efforts which have been stuck on the long-overdue handover of 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule.
A leading Palestinian, hailing Clinton's remarks, said Washington had begun playing an important role in peacemaking.

"We salute this initiative...President Clinton has realised that settlement activity is fatal to the peace process and has thus warned against it," Ahmed Korei, speaker of the 89-member Palestinian legislature, told Reuters on Tuesday.

"He has skilfully asserted the dangers of not implementing peace deals and thus I believe that the United States has begun to play an important role," Korei, better known as Abu Ala, said in the self-ruled Gaza Strip.

Israel's relations with Washington reached a 35-year low in the early 1990s over a settlement boom spearheaded by right-wing Likud party prime minister Yitzhak Shamir and his hawkish housing minister Ariel Sharon.
President Bush held up $10 billion in loan guarantees over the issue, awarding them only after Yitzhak Rabin came to power in 1992 by ousting Likud and freezing new settlement building.
Rabin, a Nobel peace laureate, was assassinated in November 1995. Netanyahu, now the Likud leader, lifted the freeze after winning election in May this year.
About 130,000 Jews live in the settlements scattered among two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

In a letter addressed to Netanyahu and made public on Monday, three former secretaries of state including Baker and five other former U.S. officials urged Israel to refrain from expanding settlements.
"We are concerned that unilateral actions, such as the expansion of settlements, would be strongly counterproductive to the goal of a negotiated solution," the letter said.
Israel and the PLO resumed talks on Hebron on Monday, prodded by Clinton who insisted the time had come for a deal.

Since a White House summit prompted by bloodshed nearly three months ago, Israel and the PLO have failed to agree on security arrangements which Netanyahu wants to protect some 400 Jews in the heart of Hebron, amid more than 100,000 Arabs.
On Monday evening Yitzhak Molcho, an adviser to Netanyahu, met Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat in Jerusalem on Hebron. A PLO official said they would resume talks on Wednesday.
